card: A 48-hour ultimatum. A small country’s reply will change the world.
intro: You are Nikola Pašić, prime minister and foreign minister of the Kingdom of Serbia. Sixty-eight years old, with a long white beard, you are the veteran leader of the Radical Party; after the Timok rebellion of 1883 you were sentenced to death in absentia and went into exile. You are known as a shrewd old politician of few words who rarely shows his hand. The two Balkan Wars (1912–1913) nearly doubled Serbia’s territory, but the army and the treasury are exhausted, and the Black Hand, a secret society of officers led by the head of military intelligence, “Apis,” is shaking your government. At your side are the twenty-five-year-old regent, Alexander; the Russian minister, Hartwig, said to be more Serbian than the Serbs; and the chief of the General Staff, Field Marshal Putnik, who leads the army in failing health. Little Serbia can lean only on Russia, and no one can say how far Russia will stand with it.

RS-00.title: A Decree and the Officer Corps

map.caption: The two Balkan Wars gave Serbia Kosovo and Macedonia in the south. Whether the army or civilian officials would govern these new territories was the issue that set the government against the officer corps in the spring of 1914.

RS-00.event: 19 April, Orthodox Easter: at a church service in Skopje, General Damjan Popović, a senior figure in the Black Hand, refused to obey the decree requiring officers to give precedence to civilian officials. When the government retired him, the officers reportedly gave him a lavish farewell banquet and, in defiance, made him head of their officers’ association.
RS-00.scene: In the spring of 1914 Interior Minister Stojan Protić issued a Priority Decree that, on its face, was a rule of protocol: at official ceremonies, civilian officials were to take precedence over officers. Its real meaning was that the government, not the army, would govern Macedonia, Kosovo and the Sanjak, the lands won in the Balkan Wars, and the officer corps took it as an insult. General Petar Bojović, speaking for the garrisons in the new territories, formally demanded with Field Marshal Putnik’s consent that the decree be amended, and King Peter I also leaned toward the army. You have already amended the decree almost entirely as the army wished, but Apis and the opposition took that only as a sign of weakness, and your majority in parliament is in danger. Two paths remain: hand the king your resignation and leave the decision to him, or give the army everything it asks.

voices.text: Withdraw the decree altogether and the government admits, in its own name, that the master of this country is not the government but the officers’ club. Better to resign and submit to the judgment of the king and the people.
Prime Minister, St Petersburg puts its trust in you. If His Majesty means to choose someone else, I will make it quite clear to him where Russia stands.

choices.text: Withdraw the decree as General Bojović demands, let army commanders run the new lands, and save the government before the election
choices.why: Better to give way and hold on until the election than lose power fighting the officers
choices.after: The officers’ club celebrated its victory, and the civilian officials in Macedonia came under the orders of army commanders. The government survived, but Apis had confirmed that it would retreat before the army.

choices.text: Resign, but first arrange for Hartwig and the crown prince to urge the king to give the government back to you
choices.why: With the Russian minister’s weight behind you, even the king cannot dismiss the government
choices.realNote: Pašić’s cabinet resigned in early June (around 2 June). Some scholars think it likely that Hartwig sided with Pašić in this crisis at Pašić’s own request.
choices.after: The king is said to have accepted the resignation gladly, but when the Russian minister Hartwig insisted strongly and France hinted that money from Paris might dry up if Pašić left, he gave the government back to you. Parliament was dissolved, the conduct of the August election passed into your hands, and on 24 June the king, citing his health, handed the exercise of royal power to Crown Prince Alexander as regent. Within days Apis’s victory had turned into defeat, and the officers’ resentment grew deeper.

note.text: The May 1903 coup ended the Obrenović dynasty, which had leaned toward Austria, and brought Peter Karađorđević, then living in exile in Geneva, to the throne. From then on Serbia’s court and its Radical governments leaned toward Russia and France, and the officers who had made him king held great sway within the army.

pressure.title: The Officers Who Made a King
pressure.text: King Peter I came back from exile to take the throne thanks to the officers who staged the coup of May 1903, and so he could not easily cross them. In this crisis, too, the king leaned toward the army, and the opposition joined hands with the officer corps to obstruct the government in parliament. Your mainstay is the Russian minister, Hartwig, who since the Balkan Wars has been said to behave like a “viceroy” in Belgrade. Black Hand circles have long disparaged you as lacking the qualities of a statesman and skilled only at party politics.

RS-01.place: Belgrade, the Foreign Ministry (office of the prime minister and foreign minister)
RS-01.title: Young Men Across the Border

map.caption: Princip and Grabež received their weapons in Belgrade, crossed the Drina by way of Šabac and Loznica, and reached Sarajevo through Tuzla.

RS-01.scene: Between late May and early June, reports from the border reach your desk. A few young Bosnians carrying weapons, they say, have crossed the Drina into Austro-Hungarian territory on the Šabac–Loznica stretch of the frontier, helped by Serbian officers and border officials. It is not hard to guess that behind them stands the officers’ society of Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, chief of intelligence on the General Staff, known as “Apis.” Yet your government has been in open conflict with those very officers over whether the army or civilian officials should govern Macedonia and Kosovo, won in the Balkan Wars. In the spring, when Interior Minister Protić issued a decree giving civilian officials precedence, the officer corps rose in protest and the cabinet even resigned for a time. Apis was at the center of the officers who stormed the palace in May 1903 and killed the Obrenović king and queen; the three bullets he took that night are still in his body.

voices.text: Prime Minister, the border officials must be called to account and the officers’ crossing routes cut. How long will you go on pretending not to know that inside the army there is a second government that does not obey the government’s orders?
Touch Apis and the whole officer corps will rise. A government facing an election cannot fight the army. Ask quietly what happened, and simply tighten the border guard.

choices.text: Remove Apis as intelligence chief and arrest Major Tankosić and the other officers involved, cutting the society’s crossing routes
choices.why: No state can stand while a second government sits inside its army
choices.after: The officers’ club in Belgrade was in uproar. Tankosić, now under arrest, had been a hero who led volunteer bands in the Balkan Wars, and officers muttered that the government was trying to please Austria.

choices.text: Treat the report as an army matter, pass it to the war minister, and avoid a second fight with the officers before the election
choices.why: With an election ahead, there is no strength left for a second fight with the army
choices.after: The report went into a drawer at the War Ministry. That the government had done nothing could one day become Vienna’s strongest evidence against Serbia.

choices.text: Have the war minister question Apis, and order border officials to stop armed men from crossing the frontier
choices.why: The crossing routes can be narrowed without a head-on clash with the officers
choices.after: The Interior Ministry ordered tighter border controls, and the war minister asked Apis for an explanation. Apis got by with a vague report implying it had been part of intelligence work, and by then the young men were already in Sarajevo.

note.text: “Unification or Death,” commonly called the Black Hand, was a secret society founded in May 1911. Estimates of its membership around 1914 vary from source to source (from a few hundred to several thousand), but most of its members were serving officers. Pijemont, a newspaper close to the society, cast Serbia as the “Piedmont” of South Slav unification, after the home region of the Kingdom of Sardinia, which led the unification of Italy.

RS-02.place: Belgrade — the Serbian legation in Vienna
RS-02.title: A Vague Warning
RS-02.scene: The newspapers have already reported that Archduke Franz Ferdinand will enter Sarajevo on 28 June after watching army maneuvers. 28 June is St Vitus’s Day, Vidovdan, which commemorates the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and is the most sorrowful and sacred day of the year for Serbs. Jovan Jovanović, your minister in Vienna, is in a position to see Biliński, the Austro-Hungarian joint finance minister responsible for administering Bosnia. The question is what he should say, and how much: the more specific he is, the more he will in effect confess, on Serbia’s behalf, that Serbian officers are involved in a plot.

voices.text: If I give names and routes, Vienna will take them as a confession by the Serbian government. A warning that the archduke’s visit is dangerous I can pass on as my personal opinion.
Vague words protect no one. If something happens, Vienna will say Serbia knew and kept silent. We must say plainly that men have crossed the border.

choices.text: On Protić’s advice, tell the Foreign Ministry in Vienna, in the government’s name, that armed young men have crossed the border
choices.why: To be accused later of knowing and keeping silent would be worse
choices.after: Vienna put the warning on record, but the archduke’s schedule did not change. The warning could one day prove Serbia’s innocence, or stand as a confession that Serbia knew of the plot.

choices.text: Let Jovanović see Biliński and hint, as his “personal opinion,” only that the archduke’s visit is dangerous
choices.why: Give a warning, but one that cannot be read as a confession by the Serbian government
choices.realNote: That Jovanović warned Biliński of danger around 21 June is broadly accepted. Albertini believes a vaguely worded telegram had earlier gone from Belgrade instructing him to give a warning, but whether it reflected Pašić’s wishes is disputed among historians.
choices.after: Jovanović later recalled saying, in effect, that one of the Bosnian Serb soldiers taking part in the maneuvers might load live rounds instead of blanks. Biliński did not take the remark seriously and is believed to have passed it on to no one.

choices.text: Since any warning would reveal the officers’ involvement, order Jovanović to say nothing at all about the archduke’s visit
choices.why: Better to appear to know nothing than to hand a hostile power a weakness
choices.after: While Belgrade said nothing, Sarajevo busied itself with preparations to welcome the archduke, and the security arrangements were astonishingly lax.

note.text: When and in what words Jovanović gave his warning is uncertain, since the account rests mainly on his own recollections of 1924. Ljuba Jovanović, minister of education in 1914, also wrote in 1924 that Pašić had told several cabinet members in late May or early June that an assassination was being prepared in Sarajevo, but this testimony too is disputed among historians.

RS-03.title: Shots on Vidovdan
RS-03.event: 24 June: citing his health, King Peter I handed royal power to his son, Crown Prince Alexander, and made him regent. Around the same time parliament was dissolved, and the general election was set for 1 August (Old Style; 14 August New Style).

telegram.text: About 10:50 a.m. / Archduke and wife shot dead / Assassin a Bosnian youth, Princip / Many accomplices arrested

RS-03.scene: News from Sarajevo reaches a Belgrade preparing to mark Vidovdan. The court and the government at once express their condolences and cancel all the day’s scheduled events. But from the next day the newspapers of Vienna and Budapest begin writing that the assassins got their weapons in Belgrade, and in Sarajevo and across Bosnia rioters attack the shops and homes of Serbs. You remember the June reports about the young men who crossed the border.

voices.text: The government must open an investigation first. If we announce an inquiry into the border officials and the officers, we take away Vienna’s pretext.
Volunteering to investigate is as good as admitting guilt. Tell Vienna to produce its evidence. Until then, admit nothing.

choices.text: Express condolences and condemnation but deny any government involvement, and admit nothing until Vienna produces evidence
choices.why: Moving first would amount to admitting guilt, and Russia does not want that either
choices.after: The Serbian government held to its position that it would investigate if the Austrian trial showed Serbian subjects to be accomplices. In Sarajevo, meanwhile, the investigators were drawing the names of Ciganović, a railway official in Belgrade, and Major Tankosić from the defendants’ statements.

choices.text: Take away Vienna’s pretext by announcing first that the government will investigate the border officials and officers involved
choices.why: The side under suspicion must act lawfully first if it is to clear itself
choices.after: The officer corps and the nationalist papers were in uproar, claiming the government had confessed to the crime. Vienna’s hard-liners, for their part, held up Serbia’s announcement as proof of complicity.

note.text: On 13 July Wiesner, the legal official sent to Sarajevo by the Austrian Foreign Ministry, reported that he had found no evidence that the Serbian government had known of or assisted in the assassination. Vienna went on preparing its ultimatum regardless of his report.

RS-03a.title: The Police Have Done Nothing Yet
RS-03a.event: 30 June: Storck, secretary of the Austro-Hungarian legation, asked Gruić, secretary general of the Foreign Ministry, what measures the Serbian police had taken or intended to take, since some of the clues to the crime lay in Serbia.
RS-03a.scene: Every day the papers in Vienna and Budapest write that the assassins got their weapons in Belgrade, and there have been repeated demonstrations outside the Serbian legation in Vienna. In Bosnia the riots against the homes and shops of Serbs go on. The Belgrade papers give no ground either: on 1 July Pijemont portrayed Princip’s deed as carrying on the resistance of Žerajić, who fired at the governor of Bosnia in 1910 and then killed himself, and called Princip a “young martyr.” Yet on your desk lies the early June report about the young men who crossed the border, and you are not the only one who knows of it.

voices.who: Wilhelm von Storck (Secretary of the Austrian Legation, telegram to Vienna, 30 June)
voices.text: The answer was that the matter has not yet engaged the attention of the Serbian police.

voices.who: Jovan Jovanović (Minister in Vienna, telegram of 1 July)
voices.text: Please do what is possible to prevent demonstrations taking place in Serbia, and to induce the Belgrade press to be as moderate as possible in tone.
You are under no obligation to answer every question Vienna asks. Put your effort into showing the newspapers and governments of Europe that Serbia is innocent.

choices.text: Through Jovanović, propose to Vienna a joint inquiry by officials of both countries, and halt Narodna Odbrana’s border activity
choices.why: Offer cooperation first, and Vienna will have less to demand
choices.after: Jovanović delivered a note from the Serbian government to the Austrian Foreign Ministry: Serbia was ready to cooperate in the investigation of the Sarajevo crime and proposed an inquiry conducted jointly by officials of both countries. In Belgrade, the government’s demand that all activity in the border districts cease was delivered to the central committee of Narodna Odbrana.

choices.text: Have the police quietly investigate Ciganović and the border network, so there is an answer ready for Storck’s inquiry
choices.why: Secure the facts through due process first, without loud announcements
choices.after: The police began tracking the railway official Ciganović, but someone tipped him off and he vanished. Major Tankosić’s unit refused to answer police questions, calling it army business.

choices.text: Condemn the crime but deny involvement, and send the legations a circular telegram to counter anti-Serbian stories in Europe
choices.why: With European opinion and Russian support, Vienna’s pressure can be withstood
choices.after: On 1 July you sent a circular telegram to the legations abroad stating that the two assassins were Austrian subjects, so Serbia had had no power to prevent the crime, and that if such elements existed in Serbia the severest measures would be taken; you instructed them to work for a swift end to the anti-Serbian campaign in the European press. The police inquiry Vienna had asked about did not begin. The same day the police seized Pijemont, but the next day the Belgrade court of first instance annulled the seizure.

note.text: In 1914 Serbia still used the Julian (Old Style) calendar of the Orthodox Church, so dates in Serbian documents run 13 days behind those of Western Europe. That is why Pašić’s circular telegrams in the Serbian Blue Book carry two dates, as in “June 18/July 1.”

pressure.title: More Than a Decade of Hostility
pressure.text: The anti-Austrian feeling in the streets of Belgrade did not arise overnight. In 1906, when Serbia concluded a customs union with Bulgaria and sought to buy its guns from France instead of Austria, Austria-Hungary blocked imports of Serbian pigs and livestock, and Serbia held out by finding new outlets through French capital and the port of Salonika. The annexation of Bosnia in October 1908 came as a great shock to those who had regarded Bosnia as land that would one day be joined to Serbia. In 1909, 53 Serbs were tried for treason in Zagreb, and at the Friedjung trial in Vienna the documents produced as evidence that politicians of the Croat-Serb Coalition had taken money from Belgrade proved to be forgeries. In a report of 15 July, Jovanović, the minister in Vienna, predicted that Vienna would use this affair to humiliate Serbia and even to justify those two trials. Against such memories, a proposal to investigate jointly with Vienna is easily read at home as surrender.

RS-04.time: Evening (the funeral was held on 14 July)
RS-04.title: The Death of Hartwig
RS-04.scene: On the evening of 10 July the Russian minister, Nikolai Hartwig, called on the Austrian minister, Giesl, to clear up ugly rumors about himself that had spread after Sarajevo, and collapsed and died of a heart attack on the spot. This Pan-Slavist, said to be more Serbian than the Serbs, had helped design the Balkan League and was the patron you trusted most. The Belgrade papers print rumors that the Austrian legation poisoned him, and the Vienna papers answer with stories that Serbian students are planning to storm the legation. The Austrian legation did in fact ask for protection, warning of an attack on the night of the king’s birthday, but nothing happened that night.

voices.who: Jovan Jovanović (Minister in Vienna, report of 6 July)
voices.text: The excitement in military and Government circles against Serbia is steadily growing owing to the tone of our press, which is diligently exploited by the Austro-Hungarian Legation at Belgrade.
The constitution guarantees freedom of the press and forbids the seizure of newspapers. If the government gags the press before an election, it hands power to the opposition.

choices.text: Explain that the constitution forbids press controls, and send the powers a circular telegram refuting the false reports
choices.why: The best answer to Vienna’s charges is a government seen to keep its constitution
choices.after: On 19 July you sent a circular telegram to all legations abroad explaining that Serbian law and the constitution guarantee the complete independence of the press and forbid the control and seizure of newspapers, so the government could not have stopped the polemics. The people of Belgrade and the entire diplomatic corps turned out for Hartwig’s funeral on 14 July, but, as you reported in your circular, order was kept.

choices.text: Give Hartwig a state funeral to display solidarity with Russia, and let citizens march shouting that he was poisoned
choices.why: Having lost a patron, Serbia must show all the more loudly that it stands with Russia
choices.after: The funeral procession was drowned in slogans denouncing Austria. Vienna’s hard-liners circulated the scene, with photographs, to newspapers across Europe.

choices.text: Heed Jovanović’s plea to calm the press: seize anti-Austrian articles and hold a quiet funeral
choices.why: Even at the cost of a constitutional row, Vienna must not be handed evidence
choices.after: Pijemont accused the government of acting as Vienna’s censor. The Vienna papers did not soften their tone, but diplomats in London and Rome took note of Belgrade’s restraint.

note.text: After Hartwig’s collapse, rumors of poisoning went around Belgrade, but a heart attack is the generally accepted cause. Giesl later wrote, in effect, that had Hartwig not died when he did, the war might have been avoided.

pressure.title: Newspapers That Cannot Be Stopped
pressure.text: Serbian law does not allow newspapers to be seized except for insulting the king or inciting revolution, and there is no censorship. Even when Pijemont was seized by the police on 1 July over an article portraying Princip as a “young martyr,” the Belgrade court of first instance annulled the seizure the next day. Austria-Hungary has banned Serbian newspapers since the annexation crisis, but Vienna’s news agency picks out only the harshest sentences in the Serbian press and spreads them across Europe. On 7 July Mali Žurnal called the archduke “a sprig of the Middle Ages” and praised Princip. Suppress the papers and the opposition gets ammunition before the election; leave them alone and Vienna gets its evidence.
pressure.src: Serbian Blue Book no. 20; Austrian dossier 1914 app. 9

RS-05.place: On the campaign trail in southern Serbia — Niš railway station
RS-05.title: An Ultimatum on the Campaign Trail
RS-05.clock: 48 hours to the deadline for a reply

telegram.text: Austrian minister delivered note in person 6 p.m. / Reply due Saturday 25th, 6 p.m. / Legation to leave if unsatisfactory / Prime minister requested to return to capital

RS-05.scene: You had been touring southern Serbia, campaigning for the August election. At 6 p.m. sharp Minister Giesl handed the note to Finance Minister Laza Pacu, who was standing in as prime minister. Its ten demands include dissolving the anti-Austrian societies, a “purge” of the schools and the officer corps, and a clause under which Austrian officials would take part in an investigation inside Serbia. When Pacu’s message came, you were on your way south to Salonika (Thessaloniki) for a short rest.

voices.who: Laza Pacu (Finance Minister and Acting Prime Minister, circular telegram to the legations abroad)
voices.text: The demands are such that no Serbian Government could accept them in their entirety.
Prime Minister, come straight back to Belgrade. A government that has received a document like this cannot be without its prime minister.

choices.text: Brush aside Pacu’s request, travel on to Salonika as planned, and gain a day without facing Vienna directly
choices.why: The prime minister’s very absence becomes a pretext for delaying the reply
choices.after: The regent and the cabinet spent the first day without the prime minister, and in the end you had to return a day late. Opposition papers mocked a prime minister who went off to rest on the day the country fell into crisis.

choices.text: Obey the regent’s summons: turn the train around, travel through the night to Belgrade, and call the cabinet at dawn
choices.why: Only if regent and cabinet speak with one voice can Serbia appeal to Russia with force
choices.realNote: Pašić is said to have meant at first to continue to Salonika and to have changed his mind about an hour after boarding the train; he was back in Belgrade in the early hours of 24 July (reportedly around 5 a.m.).
choices.after: You reached Belgrade at dawn on 24 July. The ministers had been reading the note all night, and the regent was preparing a telegram to the Tsar.

note.text: The delivery of the ultimatum was put back from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. The aim was to make sure the news reached St Petersburg only after the French president, Poincaré, then on a state visit to Russia, had sailed from Kronstadt.

RS-06.place: Belgrade, the Foreign Ministry and the Royal Palace
RS-06.title: An Appeal to St Petersburg
RS-06.clock: About 37 hours to the deadline for a reply

telegram.text: Contents of note communicated to Sazonov / German Ambassador Pourtalès: matter between Austria and Serbia only / My reply: not a question merely between Serbia and Austria, but a European question

RS-06.scene: Back at dawn, you find the ministers assembled. The army has been home from the two Balkan Wars for less than a year and is short of ammunition and rifles, and the chief of the General Staff, Field Marshal Putnik, is taking a cure at the Austrian spa of Gleichenberg. Belgrade itself is a border town: across the Sava and the Danube lies Austria-Hungary. You tell the Russian chargé d’affaires that you will hand over the reply on Saturday at 6 p.m., and the twenty-five-year-old regent signs a telegram to Nicholas II.

voices.text: We are unable to defend ourselves and we beg your Majesty to come to our aid as soon as possible.
Russia will not abandon Serbia. The crowds in the streets and the faces of the ministers all say so. Do not give in.

Sir Edward Grey’s view is clear. If it is shown that Serbian officials were accomplices in the assassination, Serbia must give full satisfaction and express regret. Accept as many of the other points as you can. That is how Europe can come down on Serbia’s side.

choices.text: Heed the ministers’ fear that the army cannot fight: tell Vienna you accept in full, without waiting for Russia’s answer
choices.why: An exhausted army could barely hold for three days, so humiliation comes cheaper than war
choices.after: The regent’s face hardened, and several ministers said they would resign. The Russian chargé d’affaires reported home that Serbia had gone down on its knees without a word to St Petersburg.

choices.text: Hold back the reply until Spalajković reports Russia’s wishes, and ask only for an extension of the deadline through the powers
choices.why: A reply written without knowing Russia’s mind will be a mistake either way
choices.after: Vienna refused the request for an extension out of hand. The day meant to buy time was simply lost, and there was even less time to write the reply.

choices.text: Ask Nicholas II for help in a telegram from the regent, and appeal to the British chargé d’affaires to get Vienna to soften
choices.why: A small country holds out only with Russian backing and British mediation together
choices.after: The regent’s telegram went to St Petersburg that day. The same day the Russian Council of Ministers decided to press, through the great powers, for an extension of the deadline. It also decided to advise Serbia, if it could not defend itself, not to resist by force but to declare that it yielded to force and entrusted its fate to the judgment of the great powers, and it authorized the war and navy ministers to ask the Tsar, as events required, to mobilize the four military districts of Kiev, Odessa, Moscow and Kazan and the Baltic and Black Sea fleets.

note.text: That day Pašić reported to Spalajković what he had said to the Russian chargé d’affaires: “I told him that the Serbian Government would appeal to the Governments of the friendly Powers to protect the independence of Serbia. If war was inevitable, I added, Serbia would carry it on.”

RS-07.title: Writing the Reply
RS-07.clock: About 8 hours to the deadline for a reply
RS-07.event: Night of 24 July to 25 July: a telegram arrives from Spalajković in St Petersburg. The Russian Council of Ministers has decided on firm measures, including mobilization, and is awaiting the Tsar’s approval; an official announcement that Russia will protect Serbia is coming soon. Among the ministers, hope spreads that Russia will not leave Serbia to its fate.
RS-07.scene: The ministers and Foreign Ministry officials worked through the night, revising sentence after sentence. The reply is to be as courteous and conciliatory in tone as possible, but the drafts lean toward attaching conditions wherever a point collides with sovereignty. Hardest of all are Point 5, which demands the “collaboration” of Austrian officials, and Point 6, under which Austrian officials would take part in a judicial investigation inside Serbia. Accept Point 6, and Austrian investigators will lay hands on the secrets of Apis and the officer corps.

voices.text: Not Point 6. If Austrian officials take part in a judicial investigation inside Serbia, this country is no longer independent, and it would violate the constitution and the code of criminal procedure.
Better to accept everything and drag out the implementation. The army is exhausted, and Russia’s promises amount to a few telegrams. Refuse, and Belgrade will be under bombardment within three days.

choices.text: Reject the whole note as a violation of sovereignty, declaring that Serbia cannot give way a third time after 1909 and 1913
choices.why: Bow a third time and both government and dynasty lose the people’s trust
choices.after: The streets of Belgrade cheered the short, defiant reply, but the foreign ministries in London and St Petersburg sighed that Serbia had handed Vienna the best pretext it could want.

choices.text: Tell Giesl you accept in principle, and buy time by first asking for talks on Points 5 and 6 and an extension
choices.why: If Vienna merely agrees to talk about interpretation, war is put off
choices.after: You held back the reply and tried to buy time. Only half a day remained, and the power to extend the deadline lay with Vienna.

choices.text: Take the minister’s point that the army is exhausted: accept all ten points, Point 6 included, and save Belgrade from bombardment
choices.why: A wound to sovereignty can heal, but a lost war cannot be undone
choices.after: The reply that came off the typewriter ran to a single page. The regent signed it without a word, and in the officers’ club the word “betrayal” began to circulate.

choices.text: Accept most demands with conditions on several, reject Point 6 as unconstitutional, and propose referral to The Hague
choices.why: Make a show of concession but keep the core of sovereignty, and Europe will take your side
choices.after: In form the reply accepted most of the demands, but it attached conditions to several points, such as “whenever the Imperial and Royal Government furnish them with facts and proofs” and “such collaboration as agrees with the principle of international law, with criminal procedure, and with good neighbourly relations,” and it refused the participation of Austrian officials under Point 6 as “a violation of the Constitution and of the law of criminal procedure.” It added that if Austria was not satisfied, Serbia was ready to refer the question to the International Tribunal of The Hague or to the great powers.

note.text: Some historians believe that Spalajković in St Petersburg reported the mood in Russia more optimistically than the facts warranted, and that his telegrams stiffened the Serbian government’s stance. No one in the Russian leadership formally promised Serbia military support.

pressure.title: No Third Humiliation
pressure.text: The note opens by reproducing word for word the Serbian government’s declaration of 31 March 1909. When Russia backed down in the annexation crisis, Serbia had to drop its protest against the annexation and promise to live on good-neighborly terms with Austria-Hungary, and the people remember it as a humiliation. In October 1913 Vienna sent an ultimatum demanding that the Serbian troops in Albania withdraw within eight days, and when even Russia’s Sazonov advised it to give way, Serbia withdrew. No one can promise that the officer corps and the voters would accept a government that bowed its head a third time.

RS-08.place: Belgrade, the Royal Palace and the Austro-Hungarian legation
RS-08.title: Mobilization and the Envelope at 5:45

map.caption: Belgrade was a border town facing the Austro-Hungarian town of Zemun (Semlin) across the Sava. On the night of 25 July the government ministries moved southeast to Niš, and parliament too was convened in Niš on 27 July.

RS-08.clock: 3 hours to the deadline for a reply
RS-08.scene: The reply is finished, but before it is handed over there is still a decision to make. Austria is poised to begin partial mobilization that evening whatever the reply says, and the Serbian capital lies within range of the batteries lined up across the Sava at Zemun. The chief of the General Staff is abroad, and if the ministries, parliament and the foreign legations are to move, they must board trains tonight. Minister Giesl’s bags are already packed, and he is ready to take the 6:30 p.m. train.

voices.text: Mobilization and concentration take days. One day late, and the enemy’s first attack falls on empty defenses along the Sava and the Danube. The capital is within artillery range of the border.
Mobilize before handing over the reply, and Vienna will say Serbia meant to fight from the start. If the reply seeks peace, the reply must go first.

choices.text: Order general mobilization, but keep the regent and the government in Belgrade so as not to appear to abandon the capital
choices.why: The moment the government leaves the capital, the morale of people and army breaks
choices.after: Citizens were relieved that the government had stayed, but the ministries’ papers and the treasury remained within range of the guns. The foreign legations sent word that they were leaving for Niš.

choices.text: With Zemun’s guns trained on the capital, order general mobilization before delivering the reply and move the government to Niš
choices.why: Vienna will move whatever the reply says, so prepare even a day sooner
choices.after: At 3 p.m. the regent ordered mobilization in the king’s name. A few minutes before the deadline (at 5:45 p.m., according to your circular telegram) you handed the reply to Giesl in person, and you told the legations abroad that “we have gone as far as was possible.” Giesl skimmed the reply, at once announced the breaking off of relations, and left for Zemun on the 6:30 p.m. train; that night the government ministries set off for Niš.

choices.text: Put off mobilization until Giesl has responded, so nothing clouds the reply’s peaceful intent, and keep the government in Belgrade
choices.why: Mobilizing first would lend weight to Vienna’s claim that Serbia meant to fight
choices.after: Giesl received the reply and still announced the break in relations and left. The mobilization order came only the next day, and the first units on the Sava line took up their positions a day late.

note.text: The Serbian army’s main field gun was the French Schneider 75 mm quick-firing gun. Serbia’s decision to buy French guns instead of Austrian Škoda guns was one of the causes of the “Pig War” (from 1906), in which Austria-Hungary blocked imports of Serbian pigs and livestock.

RS-09.title: The Field Marshal Held in Budapest

telegram.text: Field Marshal Putnik detained in Budapest on way home / By Austro-Hungarian military authorities / Release uncertain

RS-09.scene: On the evacuation train to Niš you hear the news. The chief of the General Staff, the sixty-seven-year-old Field Marshal Radomir Putnik, was on his way home from treatment for chronic emphysema at the Styrian spa of Gleichenberg when he was seized in Budapest on the evening of 25 July. The victor of the Balkan Wars, the man who drew up the Serbian army’s operational plans, is in effect in enemy hands. In Niš, a railway junction some 200 kilometers southeast of Belgrade, the ministries and foreign legations are unpacking in schools, inns and private houses.

voices.text: The army cannot move without the field marshal. Seize the Austro-Hungarian subjects in Serbia and inform Vienna that we will exchange them for him.

Reprisals only hand Vienna a pretext. Tell Europe that seizing another country’s chief of staff when war has not even been declared is against all custom. The old emperor is a man who cares about honor.

choices.text: Protest through diplomatic channels that the detention breaks all custom, and mobilize on the plan the field marshal drew up
choices.why: An appeal to the old emperor’s honor will bring the field marshal back faster than reprisals
choices.realNote: Through what channel the Serbian government protested has not been established. Putnik was released on 26 July on the orders of Foreign Minister Berchtold and at the demand of Emperor Franz Joseph.
choices.after: Emperor Franz Joseph reportedly demanded his immediate release, and the detention did not last long, but the field marshal had to travel home the long way, through Romania. Meanwhile the General Staff, following the plan prepared in advance, concentrated the army not on the border but in the Serbian interior.

choices.text: In reprisal, detain Austro-Hungarian subjects in Serbia, and tell Vienna you will exchange them for the field marshal
choices.why: If the other side broke custom first, only the same move will make Vienna back down
choices.after: Vienna claimed that Serbia had taken civilians hostage, and the field marshal’s release was delayed by several days. The tone of the London and Rome papers turned cold.

note.text: Putnik’s detention was the work of Tersztyánszky, commander of IV Corps in Budapest, with the consent of the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza. But Foreign Minister Berchtold soon ordered his release, and Emperor Franz Joseph also demanded that he be freed at once and that his strong displeasure be conveyed to whoever had ordered the detention. Some later described this “chivalry” of returning the enemy’s chief of staff as a generosity that cost Austria dearly.

RS-10.place: Niš, temporary premises of the Foreign Ministry
RS-10.title: An Open Telegram
RS-10.event: Morning of 28 July: at Potsdam, the German emperor Wilhelm II read the Serbian reply for the first time and wrote in the margin that with it “every reason for war falls away.” But that same morning Vienna sent its telegram declaring war.

telegram.at: Sent 11:10 a.m., 28 July; received at Niš 12:30 p.m.
telegram.text: Royal Serbian Government not having answered in a satisfactory manner the note of 23 July, Imperial and Royal Government compelled to have recourse to force of arms / Austria-Hungary consequently considers herself henceforward in state of war with Serbia / Berchtold

RS-10.scene: A telegram in French, not even in cipher, has come in over the ordinary telegraph. It breaks so sharply with diplomatic custom that some say its authenticity must be checked first. At the same hour Austrian batteries across the Sava at Zemun, and river monitors on the Danube, are trained on Belgrade. The regent’s appeal to the Tsar has not yet been answered. The Tsar’s reply, dated 27 July, will reach Niš only the next day, 29 July.

voices.who: Nicholas II (reply to the regent dated 27 July, received at Niš on 29 July)
voices.text: So long as the slightest hope exists of avoiding bloodshed, all our efforts must be directed to that end; but if in spite of our earnest wish we are not successful, your Highness may rest assured that Russia will in no case disinterest herself in the fate of Serbia.

voices.who: Decision of the Russian Council of Ministers (24 July; advice passed on by Sazonov through Spalajković)
voices.text: To advise the Serbian Government, in case the situation of Serbia should be such that she could not with her own strength protect herself against the possible armed invasion by Austria-Hungary, not to offer armed resistance to the invasion of Serbian territory, if such an invasion should occur, but to announce that Serbia yields to force and that she entrusts her fate to the judgment of the Great Powers.
Prime Minister, issue a proclamation to the people in the king’s name. Serbia has fought two wars and never once retreated.

choices.text: As the Russian Council of Ministers advised, offer no armed resistance and declare that Serbia leaves its fate to the great powers
choices.why: Give up the capital but save the army and the state, and the powers will keep Serbia independent
choices.after: The Serbian army pulled back from the Sava and the Danube and stayed in the interior. As he signed the declaration the regent said, “This is not a surrender but an appeal to Europe,” and in the officers’ club talk of a coup began to circulate openly.

choices.text: Once the telegram is confirmed, proclaim a war of defense in the king’s name, and inform Russia and the Entente at once
choices.why: Only if Serbia fights will Russia be unable to stay indifferent to its fate
choices.after: At 2:10 p.m. you sent an urgent telegram from Niš to Spalajković, and that same day Spalajković petitioned Sazonov, asking that Russia punish this act committed against “a small Slav country which only recently emerged from a long series of heroic, but exhausting battles.” That night the Serbian army blew up the railway bridge over the Sava, and from about 2 a.m. on 29 July the Austrian river monitors and the Zemun batteries began shelling Belgrade.

note.text: The Austro-Hungarian invasion of Serbia began in earnest only on 12 August. Declaring war two weeks before the army was ready was meant to create a fait accompli before the great powers could step in to mediate.

RS-10a.place: Niš, temporary premises of the Foreign Ministry
RS-10a.title: Breaking with Berlin

map.caption: In early August Europe went to war in two camps, Germany and Austria-Hungary against Russia, France and Britain, and on 6 August Serbia broke off relations with Germany as well.

RS-10a.event: Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and on 4 August Britain declared war on Germany. Montenegro too declared war on Austria-Hungary around 5 August.
RS-10a.scene: Germany, Austria-Hungary’s ally, has not yet declared war on Serbia, and the German minister, Griesinger, is staying in Niš with the rest of the diplomatic corps. The Serbian chargé d’affaires in Berlin is also still in the German capital. Now that all Europe has split into two camps, even small Serbia must decide whether to keep its link with Germany or stand clearly with Russia and its allies. Across the Drina, the Austro-Hungarian army is hurrying to concentrate.

voices.text: Cut our link with Germany as well, and we lose our channel to the only country that can restrain Vienna. Germany has not even declared war first. Why shut the door?
Russia has gone to war with Germany because of Serbia. If Serbia keeps its legation in Berlin, St Petersburg will take it as betrayal.

choices.text: Return the German minister’s passports and withdraw the legation in Berlin, standing clearly with Russia and its allies
choices.why: With Russia fighting for Serbia’s sake, hesitating now would cost Serbia its ally
choices.after: On 4 August you ordered the chargé d’affaires in Berlin to leave Germany at once with his staff, and on 6 August the Foreign Ministry informed the German legation in Niš that, “in view of the solidarity of her interests with Russia and her allies,” the minister’s mission was at an end, and sent him his passports. In Berlin the under secretary of state at the Foreign Office, Zimmermann, told the departing Serbian chargé d’affaires that all the responsibility lay with Russia, which had egged Serbia on, and that Austria would probably have been satisfied with occupying Belgrade.

choices.text: Since Germany has not yet declared war, keep Minister Griesinger in Niš and sound out a ceasefire with Vienna through Berlin
choices.why: The channel to the only country that can restrain Vienna must be kept open to the last
choices.after: Griesinger passed Serbia’s wishes on to his government, but Berlin, now fighting on two fronts, replied only that Serbia should talk to Vienna directly. From St Petersburg, Spalajković reported Sazonov’s cold reaction.

note.text: Soon after the war began, when the Social Democrat Dragiša Lapčević protested that the government had tolerated the secret organization that brought on the war, Pašić reportedly replied that such an organization did exist but was not yet very dangerous, and that if it really became dangerous the government would take the necessary measures. Lapčević recounted this conversation in an article in Politika in 1926.

pressure.title: Russia’s Proxy?
pressure.text: Vienna and Berlin portrayed Serbia as Russia’s tool, and the German under secretary for foreign affairs, Zimmermann, told the departing Serbian chargé d’affaires that all the responsibility lay with Russia, which had egged Serbia on. But Russia did not move Serbia at will. In the Albanian crisis of 1913 Russia did not back Serbia to the end, and on 4 July Sazonov advised that the most important thing was for Serbian public opinion to stay calm. On 24 July the Russian Council of Ministers even decided to advise Serbia not to resist by force if it could not defend itself, but the Russian chargé d’affaires in Belgrade, instructed to pass on this advice at his discretion, did not convey it to the Serbian government (Sazonov told Spalajković the same thing directly). One interpretation holds that Serbia’s choices sprang less from Russian orders than from the hopes it placed in Russia and from domestic politics.

RS-11.place: Western Serbia, the Mačva plain and Mount Cer
RS-11.title: Night on Mount Cer

map.caption: On 12 August the Austro-Hungarian Fifth Army crossed the lower Drina from Bosnia into western Serbia; defeated on Mount Cer and the Mačva plain on 15–24 August, it withdrew.

RS-11.event: 12 August: the Austro-Hungarian army, with the Fifth Army as its main force, crossed the Drina and the Sava and invaded Serbia. The commander of the invasion was Potiorek, the governor of Bosnia, who had been responsible for the archduke’s security in Sarajevo.
RS-11.scene: Field Marshal Putnik, home at last by way of Romania, never meant to defend the whole long frontier from the start. The Serbian army gathered in the interior to wait and see where the enemy’s main thrust would come, and at first the field marshal thought it would come from the north. But the enemy’s main force is crossing the Drina in the west and pushing toward the Mačva plain and Mount Cer. Rifles are short even in the front-line units, and many of the older third-levy reservists turned out with only a greatcoat and cap in place of a uniform, or in peasant clothes with leather opanci on their feet.

voices.who: Radomir Putnik (Field Marshal, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command)
voices.text: The main thrust is on the Drina. Stepanović’s Second Army must be turned toward Mount Cer overnight. One day late, and the enemy opens the road to Valjevo.
Strip the Sava front in the north and the capital, and Belgrade falls. Are you proposing that we give up the capital?

choices.text: With the enemy’s main force massed in the west, send the First Army across the Sava in the north into Srem to turn the enemy back
choices.why: Defense alone cannot win; only a blow on enemy soil will force a retreat
choices.after: While the army swung north, the enemy on the Drina pushed deep into Serbia. In fact, the Serbian offensive into Srem came only in September, after the victory at Cer, and was soon pulled back.

choices.text: In case the Sava attack is the main thrust, hold the north and the capital in strength, and fight a delaying action in the west
choices.why: Safer not to divide the army until the enemy’s main thrust is certain
choices.after: As the Drina line gave way, the enemy came close to Valjevo. The Serbian army did counterattack in the end, but at the cost of heavier casualties and more ammunition.

choices.text: As Field Marshal Putnik judges, turn the Second Army toward Mount Cer overnight and strike the enemy’s main force across the Drina
choices.why: Only by breaking the enemy’s main force first can both the capital and the north be saved
choices.after: The battle that began on the slopes of Mount Cer in a downpour on the night of 15 August ended with the recapture of Šabac on 24 August. The Austro-Hungarian army withdrew from Serbia, and the victory is counted as the first Allied victory of the First World War. For it, Stepa Stepanović, commander of the Second Army, was promoted to field marshal (vojvoda).

note.text: Deaths at Cer are estimated at 3,000 to 5,000 on the Serbian side and 6,000 to 10,000 on the Austro-Hungarian side (with about 4,500 taken prisoner), and the figures vary from study to study. The victory used up the army’s ammunition, and the shortage remained the Serbian army’s greatest weakness all autumn.

RS-12.place: Serbian Supreme Command — the government at Niš
RS-12.title: An Offensive the Allies Asked For

map.caption: In early September the Serbian First Army crossed the Sava into Srem, while the Austro-Hungarian army crossed the Drina again (near Loznica). The Užice Army and the Montenegrin army entered eastern Bosnia and advanced toward Sarajevo.

RS-12.event: Late August to early September: Russian and Austro-Hungarian armies clashed on a vast scale in Galicia to the east, and on 3 September the Russians entered Lemberg.
RS-12.scene: Two weeks after the victory at Cer, the Entente asks Serbia to cross the Sava and advance into Austrian Srem, to hold back as much as possible of the Austro-Hungarian Second Army, which is moving to the Russian front. But the Serbian army used up nearly all its ammunition at Cer, and it has a single shell factory turning out little more than 100 rounds a day. Across the Drina, Potiorek is preparing a second invasion, and some officers say that a push into eastern Bosnia would open the road to Sarajevo.

voices.who: Radomir Putnik (Field Marshal, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command)
voices.text: An offensive without ammunition only sheds blood. But if the alliance collapses, Serbia will not survive either. If it must be done, it must be short and limited.
If Serbia only defends itself while the Russian army bleeds in Galicia, St Petersburg and Paris will ask whom Serbia is fighting for.

choices.text: Grant the Russian and French request and send the First Army across the Sava into Srem, short of ammunition as it is
choices.why: If the alliance falls, Serbia falls with it, so the burden must be shared
choices.after: Around 6 September the Serbian army crossed the Sava, and one column took Zemun. But the Timok I Division of the Second Army, sent across in a diversionary crossing, was shattered with some 6,000 casualties, and when the Austro-Hungarian army crossed the Drina again on the night of 7–8 September, Putnik called the First Army back south. Meanwhile the Užice Army and the Montenegrin Sanjak Army took Višegrad in eastern Bosnia on 14 September, but the offensive came to a halt before it reached Sarajevo.

choices.text: Enter eastern Bosnia with the Montenegrin army, call on the Serb population to rise, and make for Sarajevo
choices.why: Striking Bosnia directly brings the goal of South Slav unification closer
choices.after: The Serbian and Montenegrin armies pushed deep toward Sarajevo, but they had to fall back when the enemy, crossing the lower Drina, threatened their rear. In the border villages, people who had joined the rising suffered reprisals from the Austro-Hungarian army.

choices.text: Decline the request, citing a shell factory that turns out little more than 100 rounds a day, and strengthen the Drina line
choices.why: Stopping the coming second invasion matters more than someone else’s front
choices.after: The Serbian army met the second invasion on the Drina line and was spared the losses of the Timok Division. But in Paris and St Petersburg there were complaints that Serbia would not share the burden of the alliance.

note.text: In the Battle of the Drina, which began on 7 September, the Serbian army suffered heavy losses on the Mačkov Kamen height of Mount Jagodnja, where for four days frontal attacks and counterattacks followed one another. The front soon hardened into trench warfare, and for Serbian infantry wearing opanci instead of boots, the trenches in the autumn rain were as harsh as the lack of ammunition.

RS-11N.title: Left to the Powers
RS-11N.scene: When the Serbian army withdrew without a fight, Austrian troops entered Belgrade in early August. Vienna holds the capital as a “pledge” and says it will stay until Serbia has carried out every demand of the ultimatum. The German emperor’s proposal of 28 July, to “halt in Belgrade,” has unexpectedly come true. Russia’s case for going as far as general mobilization for a Serbia that does not fight has weakened, and a conference of ambassadors is about to open in London.

voices.text: A government that gives up the capital without firing a shot is no government. The officers will not forget this humiliation.
Sir Edward Grey says he will work to see that the London conference guarantees Serbia’s independence. But Serbia must accept the conference’s decisions.

choices.text: While awaiting the conference, have Field Marshal Putnik rebuild the army in the south, and calm the angry officer corps
choices.why: However the conference ends, Serbia can hold firm in negotiation only with its army intact
choices.after: Field Marshal Putnik rebuilt the army around Niš and Kragujevac. The officers’ anger did not subside, but the army remained intact.

choices.text: As Grey’s message through Crackanthorpe asks, entrust Serbia’s fate to the London conference and promise to abide by its decision
choices.why: To win a guarantee from the powers, Serbia must first promise to accept their decision
choices.after: The ambassadors of the great powers gathered in London. Serbia, its capital surrendered, now waits for a verdict on its own fate.

note.text: In fact, in a handwritten letter to Jagow on the morning of 28 July, Wilhelm II proposed that the Austrian army occupy Belgrade as a pledge, halt there, and see whether Serbia kept its promises. In Vienna the proposal was in effect ignored.

RS-04M.place: Belgrade — the Foreign Ministry in Vienna (the Ballhausplatz)
RS-04M.title: A Hand Held Out First
RS-04M.event: 3 July: the funeral mass for the archduke and his wife was held in the court chapel in Vienna. The day before, when the remains arrived in Vienna and Jovanović flew the legation’s flag at half-mast in mourning, the landlord and neighbors demanded that it be taken down, and demonstrations went on outside the legation through the night.
RS-04M.scene: The Ballhausplatz has received Serbia’s proposal of a joint inquiry but has not replied. Under Secretary Macchio tells Jovanović only that the judicial investigation in Sarajevo is still under way and that Serbia should first punish the agitators on its own soil. Vienna knows that once it agrees to investigate jointly with Serbia, its own options narrow. In Belgrade, figures close to Narodna Odbrana protest that the government has abandoned its brothers in Bosnia, and Pijemont calls your government “Vienna’s police.”

voices.who: Serbian government declaration of 31 March 1909 (the words quoted again at the head of the note of 23 July)
voices.text: Serbia undertakes, moreover, to modify the direction of her policy with regard to Austria-Hungary and to live in future on good neighbourly terms with the latter.
Vienna will neither accept the proposal nor reject it; it will play for time. Before the proposal vanishes into a drawer, we must make it known in the capitals of the powers.
Words alone will not persuade Vienna. Arrest Ciganović and summon Tankosić for questioning, and the proposal will be seen to be sincere.

choices.text: As Jovanović advises, make the proposal known in London, Paris, Rome and St Petersburg, so that Vienna cannot easily ignore it
choices.why: With the powers watching, Vienna cannot bury the proposal in a drawer
choices.after: Grey called Serbia’s proposal reasonable, and Sazonov too said Vienna had no reason to reject it. But Berlin advised Vienna not to be taken in by Serbia’s delaying tactics.

choices.text: As Protić advises, arrest Ciganović and summon Major Tankosić, proving by deeds that the proposal is sincere
choices.why: A proposal of words alone reads as stalling, so Serbia must act first
choices.after: Ciganović was caught fleeing toward Montenegro, and Tankosić answered the government’s summons but would say nothing. In the officers’ club there was talk that the government was doing the work of Austrian investigators.

note.text: Narodna Odbrana was founded on 8 October 1908, just after the annexation, by ministers, officials and generals meeting at Belgrade city hall; after Serbia accepted the annexation in 1909 it presented itself as a cultural society. But its membership overlapped with the Black Hand’s, and the ultimatum of 23 July demanded the dissolution not of the Black Hand, which had directed the preparations for the assassination, but of this society.

RS-05M.title: A Showdown Without a Patron
RS-05M.event: Evening of 10 July: the Russian minister, Hartwig, called at the Austrian legation and died of a heart attack on the spot (as in fact happened).
RS-05M.scene: With your most trusted patron gone, the anger of the officer corps breaks into the open. Apis’s comrades call the government’s halting of Narodna Odbrana and its offer of a joint inquiry to Vienna a betrayal of the nation, and some officers speak of the night of 1903. Regent Alexander wants to seize the moment to remove Apis as intelligence chief; War Minister Stefanović urges against it, saying the army cannot be split in two a month before the election.

voices.text: Prime Minister, leave Apis in that post and neither your proposal nor my regency will last long. Send him to a provincial unit.
The moment you touch Apis, the intelligence department’s border network slips out of the government’s hands and goes underground. Wait until the election is over.

choices.text: As Stefanović advises, leave Apis in his post but agree with the officers that Interior Ministry civilians will police the border
choices.why: Better to secure the border than to split the army in two before the election
choices.after: Apis kept his post, and border security passed to the Interior Ministry. Vienna concluded that the Serbian government would never dare touch the society.

choices.text: Accept the regent’s wish: remove Apis as intelligence chief and send him to a provincial unit near Niš before the election
choices.why: With the patron gone, the government survives only by curbing the society first
choices.after: Apis received orders transferring him to a unit near Niš, and the officers’ club fell quiet for several days. No one can say for sure what the silence means.

note.text: In fact, Vienna discussed a hard line against Serbia at a joint council of ministers on 7 July, and the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza, who had at first objected, agreed on 14 July to the course of an ultimatum. Many historians hold that once Berlin’s backing had been secured (5–6 July), Vienna’s decision was already hardening whatever Serbia did.

RS-06M.title: The Note Comes All the Same
RS-06M.clock: 48 hours to the deadline for a reply
RS-06M.scene: Minister Giesl hands over the note. Vienna has not given Serbia’s proposal of a joint inquiry a single line, and the ten demands and the 48-hour deadline are unchanged. This time, though, the foreign ministries of Europe have on record that Serbia proposed a joint inquiry three weeks earlier. The heaviest demand is still Point 6, under which Austrian officials would take part in an investigation inside Serbia.

voices.text: It was Serbia that first raised a joint inquiry. Reject Point 6 out of hand and that proposal becomes empty words. Find a way to accept it within Serbian law.

What Serbia proposed was a mixed inquiry between equals, not Austrian officials interrogating Serbian officers. Accept Point 6 as it stands and we break the constitution and the code of criminal procedure.

choices.text: As Protić says, reject Point 6 as unconstitutional, and ask for arbitration at The Hague if Vienna is not satisfied
choices.why: Serbia offered an inquiry between equals, not interrogation by foreign officials
choices.after: The reply took the same course as the one Serbia actually sent. The proposal of three weeks earlier helped win Europe’s sympathy but did not change Vienna’s decision.

choices.text: As the regent says, offer to accept Point 6 through a mixed commission chaired by a Serbian judge, building on Serbia’s offer
choices.why: Carrying the joint inquiry forward within the law keeps Serbia’s case strong
choices.after: The reply was almost the same as the one Serbia actually sent, but on Point 6 it proposed a mixed commission chaired by a Serbian judge, with Austrian officials taking part. Under instructions to leave unless the acceptance was unconditional, Giesl announced the break in relations and left, but the concrete alternative of a mixed commission was at once made known in London and Berlin.

choices.text: Keep the word Serbia gave when it proposed a joint inquiry: accept all ten points, Point 6 included, unconditionally
choices.why: Consistency to the end protects the country better than going back on an offer
choices.after: You signed a reply that accepted even Point 6. The word “betrayal” circulated again in the officers’ club, and the regent said nothing all day.

note.text: The international commission of inquiry created by the 1899 Hague Convention was used after the Dogger Bank incident of 1904, when the Russian fleet fired on British trawlers in the North Sea, to prevent a clash between Britain and Russia. Some interpret the mention of the International Tribunal of The Hague in Serbia’s actual reply as made with such precedents in mind.

RS-07M.title: A Mixed Commission in Belgrade
RS-07M.event: Morning of 28 July: at Potsdam, Wilhelm II read the Serbian reply and wrote in the margin that with it the reason for war had vanished. The emperor did in fact write a similar note that same morning.
RS-07M.scene: Conrad, the Austro-Hungarian chief of the General Staff, calls the mixed commission a delaying tactic and urges speedy mobilization, but Vienna, pressed at once from Berlin and London, has put off declaring war and sent its terms through the British legation. Austrian officials are to join the commission and investigate every name that appears in the statements of the Sarajevo defendants, with no exception for soldiers. Follow the statements, and they lead to Major Tankosić and those above him, up to the chief of intelligence on the General Staff, Apis. Serbia’s preparations for mobilization have not stopped either.

voices.text: Sir Edward Grey says he will work for the four powers to guarantee Serbia’s independence while the commission sits. Do not let this chance slip.
The day a Serbian officer is made to stand before Austrian officials, the officers lose any reason to protect this government.

choices.text: Have the commission stop at civilians and junior officers, and shield Apis and the General Staff chiefs, citing military secrecy
choices.why: Saving the commission is no use if handing over the army’s leaders brings down the government
choices.after: The commission stopped after examining Ciganović and a few border officials. Conrad declared that Serbia had covered up the truth and that he would wait for the next opportunity.

choices.text: Trusting Crackanthorpe’s word on a guarantee, hand even Apis and the officers to the commission, with the regent holding the Guard
choices.why: With a guarantee from the powers at stake, save the commission even at the cost of the society
choices.after: Apis, summoned before the commission, refused to testify, citing the secrecy of intelligence work, and the commission recommended that he be handed over to a Serbian court-martial. Several barracks stirred, but the Royal Guard stood by the regent.

note.text: In fact, in a handwritten letter to Jagow on the morning of 28 July, Wilhelm II proposed that the Austrian army occupy Belgrade as a pledge, halt there, and see whether Serbia kept its promises. But Vienna sent its declaration of war that same day. Since Vienna had already ordered partial mobilization on 25 July and Berchtold considered any compromise too late, many historians think it unlikely that Vienna would have accepted a mixed commission.

RS-08M.title: The Price of a Managed Crisis
RS-08M.scene: On election day, the Independent Radicals and the nationalist papers attack the government for letting Austrian officials onto Serbian soil, while your supporters say it kept the new territories without a war. Peasants who lost sons and brothers in the Balkan Wars are relieved to have escaped a third war, but the officers’ resentment has not subsided. The negotiations with Vienna since the spring over the Oriental Railway and the transit of Austrian goods have shown that other bargains are possible too. But the question of the Serbs of Bosnia remains, and no commission has been able to settle it.

voices.text: Stand on your record as the government that kept the peace. Promise to conclude the trade and railway negotiations with Vienna, so that the country never again goes through anything like the Pig War.
A government that bowed its head before Austrian officials has no right to speak of a South Slav Piedmont.

choices.text: As Protić urges, campaign on peace and reconstruction, pledging to conclude the trade and railway negotiations with Vienna
choices.why: Weary peasants will vote for the government that spared them a war
choices.after: The Radicals lost seats but kept power. You sent a trade delegation to Vienna and asked Paris for a loan to build railways in the new territories.

choices.text: To fend off the Independent Radicals, pledge the South Slav cause and rearmament, and win back the officer corps
choices.why: Give up the national cause and both the election and the army go to the opposition
choices.after: The Radicals won comfortably. But the General Staff in Vienna noted Serbia’s pledge to rearm as grounds for the next crisis.

note.text: A memorandum on the Balkan situation prepared by the Foreign Ministry in Vienna in June 1914 warned of Serbia as the South Slav “Piedmont,” yet recorded that negotiations with Serbia over the sale of Oriental Railway Company shares had just been concluded. The channels for economic bargains between Serbia and Austria-Hungary were not entirely closed.

RS-02P.title: The Officers Strike Back
RS-02P.scene: Major Tankosić’s arrest sets the officers’ club and Pijemont in uproar. Apis’s comrades accuse the government of jailing national heroes to please Austria, and in some units there is even talk of refusing the government’s orders. Everyone in Belgrade knows that the officers who killed a king and changed the dynasty in 1903 could move again. Crown Prince Alexander distrusts Apis’s faction, and the Russian minister, Hartwig, backs your government.

voices.who: Dragutin Dimitrijević, “Apis” (Chief of Intelligence, General Staff)
voices.text: Prime Minister, the army is not the government’s servant; it is the sword of the nation. If you jail officers for helping our brothers in Bosnia, the officers have no reason to protect this government.
Give in to the army and this country will have no government. Russia wants an orderly Serbia. But end the commotion quickly.

choices.text: Release Tankosić in view of the unrest in the units, but have the Interior Ministry quietly tighten border control
choices.why: A head-on clash with the army would topple the government first, so step back
choices.after: Tankosić was released, and the officers laughed that the government had lost its nerve. The crisis passed, but any chance of bringing back the young men who had crossed the border was gone.

choices.text: Hold firm with the crown prince and Hartwig behind you: transfer Apis to the provinces and announce a court-martial
choices.why: Curb the society while the crown prince and Russia stand behind you
choices.after: Apis was transferred to a unit in Niš. The officers’ club fell silent, but many said that made it all the more unsettling.

note.text: In the coup of May 1903 (in the early hours of 11 June, New Style), officers led by Apis killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga, and parliament hailed him as “savior of the fatherland.” His nickname “Apis” is said by some to come from the Egyptian bull god (for his powerful build) and by others from the Latin word for bee (for his industry).

RS-03P.title: A Warning with Names
RS-03P.scene: The arrested officer’s statement reveals that a few young Bosnians crossed the border carrying Belgian-made Browning pistols and grenades from the Kragujevac arsenal. They are already inside Austro-Hungarian territory. On 28 June, Vidovdan, Archduke Franz Ferdinand is to enter Sarajevo. A warning might save the archduke, but it would mean the Serbian government admitting in writing that Serbian officers were involved.

voices.text: If we give names and routes, Vienna will have proof in its hands that Serbian officers were involved. It may save the archduke’s life, but Vienna will have a hold over Serbia.
If the archduke falls to Serbian weapons, what Vienna demands then will not be a few names but the whole of Serbia’s sovereignty.

choices.text: Formally pass to Vienna the weapons and names confirmed by Tankosić’s statement, and offer to cooperate in the investigation
choices.why: Next to the price paid if the archduke falls, a few names come cheap
choices.after: The warning reached Biliński and Governor Potiorek in Sarajevo. But the archduke’s entourage, used to countless threats, decided not to change his schedule.

choices.text: Tell Vienna only about the weapons and the border crossing, and, as Jovanović fears, withhold the officers’ names
choices.why: Fulfill the duty to warn, but do not hand Vienna the evidence as well
choices.after: Vienna received the warning but gave it little weight, calling its source vague. The archduke’s visit to Sarajevo went ahead as planned.

note.text: The actual assassins carried four pistols and six grenades. The pistols were Brownings made by the Belgian firm FN, and the grenades came from the Serbian arsenal at Kragujevac.

RS-04P.title: Preemptive Steps After the Shots
RS-04P.scene: On the morning of 28 June, despite the warning, the archduke’s motorcade passed through the streets of Sarajevo as planned, and Princip’s bullets killed the archduke and his wife. The Vienna papers name Serbia as the culprit. But this time the record shows that Serbia had already arrested officers and even warned Vienna, and the foreign legations in Belgrade know it.

voices.text: Your warning will protect Serbia. But let Austrian officials into Serbia’s investigation, and next they will be demanding to investigate the Serbian army.
Put the arrested officers on public trial and allow foreign diplomats to attend. Serbia must show Europe that it has nothing to hide.

choices.text: Hold the trial behind closed doors in a Serbian court, keeping out the foreign interference Hartwig fears
choices.why: Let foreign eyes in once, and next they will be looking into the army
choices.after: The trial began behind closed doors. Vienna suspected Serbia of trying to cover up the truth.

choices.text: As Protić urges, put the arrested officers on public trial and allow British, French and Italian diplomats to attend
choices.why: Showing Europe there is nothing to hide is the best defense
choices.after: British, French and Italian diplomats took their seats in the public gallery of the Belgrade court. Vienna’s hard-liners had to rewrite their indictment of Serbia.

note.text: Because Princip was not yet twenty at the time of the crime, he escaped the death penalty and was sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment; he died of tuberculosis in the fortress prison of Theresienstadt in April 1918.

RS-04Q.title: What to Do About Narodna Odbrana
RS-04Q.event: Early July: the Hungarian news agency and the Budapest papers reported that the Sarajevo defendants had been in the pay of Narodna Odbrana in Belgrade. The official news agency in Vienna said the investigation was strictly secret and warned against taking such reports at face value, but the accusations did not stop.
RS-04Q.scene: As the trial of the arrested officers gets under way, Vienna’s accusations turn toward Narodna Odbrana, a far better-known name than the Black Hand. The society was founded by ministers and generals together just after the annexation in 1908, and since 1909 it has presented itself as a cultural society, but its network and membership in the border districts still overlap with the Black Hand’s. Wind it up and one of the biggest pretexts Vienna could use disappears, but its leadership includes generals of the Balkan Wars and well-known writers.

voices.text: At least dissolve the border committees and publish the statutes and the accounts. Show that there is nothing to hide, and Vienna loses the first page of its indictment.

voices.who: A member of the Narodna Odbrana central committee
voices.text: This society has run schools, lectures and gymnastic associations for the nation. Dissolve it to suit Vienna’s accusations, and the government admits that what the Austrian papers say is true.

choices.text: As Protić urges, dissolve the border committees and publish the statutes and accounts, leaving the society purely cultural
choices.why: Tearing out the first page of Vienna’s indictment now costs far less
choices.after: Narodna Odbrana announced that it had dissolved its committees in the border districts. The Vienna papers called it a sham, but diplomats from London and Rome reported home that Belgrade had moved first.

choices.text: Leave alone a lawful society led by generals and writers, and rebut Vienna’s charges as baseless propaganda in a circular telegram
choices.why: Dissolving the society to suit Vienna would admit that its charges are true
choices.after: The government circulated a telegram stating that Narodna Odbrana was a lawful cultural society. But the society’s name will head the indictment Vienna is preparing.

note.text: A pamphlet published by Narodna Odbrana’s central committee in 1911 listed its aims at its founding in 1908 as rousing national feeling, enrolling volunteers and forming volunteer units, and organizing special armed bands (komitadji), and stated that once the annexation had been recognized, its new aim was to prepare the people for war through “all forms of national work,” such as gymnastics and education. In the dossier it circulated to the powers after the ultimatum, Austria-Hungary used this pamphlet as evidence of Serbian agitation.

RS-05P.title: A Softer Note
RS-05P.clock: 48 hours to the deadline for a reply
RS-05P.event: 10 July: the Russian minister, Hartwig, called at the Austrian legation and died of a heart attack (as in fact happened).
RS-05P.scene: Vienna’s hard-liners still wanted war, but the fact that Serbia had already punished the culprits and even given a warning strengthened the objections of the Hungarian prime minister, Tisza. The note Minister Giesl handed over carried a 48-hour deadline, but it went no further than demanding the dissolution of the anti-Austrian societies and the formation of a mixed commission of inquiry. Admitting Austrian officials to the commission still collides with the Serbian constitution.

voices.text: Prime Minister, Austrian officials interrogating Serbian officers on Serbian soil is the one thing we cannot accept. The people would never forgive the dynasty.
St Petersburg hopes Serbia will concede as much as it can and gain time. If the commission were international, Russia too could insist on taking part.

choices.text: Accept the mixed commission of inquiry with Austria as it stands, since rejecting even a softer note would forfeit Serbia’s case
choices.why: Vienna has given this much ground; ending it here costs the least
choices.after: Austrian investigators arrived in Belgrade. The crisis subsided, but the officer corps seethed with anger.

choices.text: As the regent wishes, dissolve the societies but reject a mixed commission with Austrian officials as a breach of sovereignty
choices.why: With the culprits already on trial, there is no reason to retreat further
choices.after: Vienna’s hard-liners talked of war again, but because Serbia had already put the culprits on trial, they could not win over Tisza and the old emperor.

choices.text: Take Strandtmann’s hint and counter with an international commission of inquiry including all the great powers, not Austria alone
choices.why: With Russia on the commission too, the blow to sovereignty is shared
choices.after: Grey and Sazonov at once backed the counterproposal, and Vienna, to avoid isolation, agreed to negotiate.

note.text: After Hartwig’s death, the Russian legation in Belgrade was headed throughout the July Crisis by the chargé d’affaires, Vasily Strandtmann. The Serbian government had in effect lost its most experienced patron in the middle of the crisis.

RS-06P.title: The Colonel with the Sword
RS-06P.scene: As the crisis subsides, the anger of the officer corps erupts. Intelligence comes in that comrades of the transferred Apis are plotting a coup to bring down the government, and Pijemont calls you “Vienna’s servant.” Regent Alexander, who remembers the night of 1903, wants to root out the society once and for all.

voices.text: Prime Minister, leave the society as it is and the next bullet will be fired at this palace. Send them before a court-martial.
Put the heroes of the Balkan Wars before a court-martial and the army will split in two. Stop at sending Apis abroad as a military attaché.

choices.text: As Stefanović advises, send Apis abroad as a military attaché and quietly dissolve the society without a trial
choices.why: Better to remove the heroes quietly than split the army by putting them on trial
choices.after: Apis left to become military attaché in a distant country. The society scattered, but no one knows whether its network has gone with it.

choices.text: As the regent wishes, use the coup intelligence to court-martial Apis and the society’s leaders for treason
choices.why: Fail to finish the society now, and the next bullet will be aimed at the palace
choices.after: In court Apis proclaimed the cause of South Slav unification to the end. The society was broken, but young officers who saw him as a martyr remained.

note.text: In fact, Pašić and the regent had Apis arrested in exile in December 1916, and the following year a court-martial at Salonika sentenced him to death. Apis was shot on 26 June 1917 and rehabilitated at a retrial in 1953.
