RS-07P.place: Across Serbia — campaign rallies in Niš and Belgrade
RS-07P.title: The Price of Peace
RS-07P.scene: On election day, the Independent Radicals and the nationalist papers attack the Radical government for going down on its knees before Austria, while your supporters say it kept the new territories without a war. The two Balkan Wars greatly enlarged Serbia’s territory and population, but there are not enough officials to govern the new lands, nor rifles to rearm the army. Peasants who endured the “Pig War,” when Austria blocked imports of Serbian pigs for several years from 1906, want above all a peaceful harvest.

voices.text: Building schools and railways in the new territories alone will take ten years. Campaign on peace. The peasants do not want a third war.
South Slav unification is Serbia’s mission. A government that bowed its head to Vienna has no right to be the Piedmont of the South Slavs.

choices.text: As Protić urges, campaign on peace and rebuilding the new lands, and build railways and schools with French and Russian loans
choices.why: What the peasants want is not a third war but a peaceful harvest
choices.after: The Radicals narrowly held their majority. You sent delegations to Paris and St Petersburg to negotiate loans.

choices.text: To keep the national cause from the Independent Radicals, take up South Slav unification again and pledge to rearm
choices.why: To erase the stigma of surrender, Serbia must seize the national cause again
choices.after: The Radicals won comfortably. But Vienna noted Serbia’s pledge to rearm as grounds for the next crisis.

note.text: The two Balkan Wars (1912–1913) enlarged Serbia’s territory from about 48,000 km² to 87,000 km², a little over 1.8 times, and its population from about 2.9 million to 4.4–4.5 million. Whether the new territories should be under military or civilian rule was the central issue in the clash between the government and the officer corps in the spring of 1914.

RS-08P.title: A Bargain with Vienna
RS-08P.scene: With the election over and the crisis subsiding, the Austrian legation raises the question of trade negotiations again. Since the spring the two governments had been working through the question of the Oriental Railway, new rail links and the transit of Austrian goods across Serbia, so a path does exist. When Austria closed the border during the Pig War, Serbia held out by finding new outlets through French capital and the port of Salonika, and the peasants have not forgotten those hard years. Joining hands with Vienna would open the Bosnian and Hungarian markets wider, but the nationalists would call it a second surrender after 1909.

voices.text: Building railways and schools in the new territories takes money. A new trade and railway agreement with Vienna would rescue the treasury and open a way to pay the interest on the French loans.
The moment Serbia leans on Vienna’s market again, it goes back to being Austria’s economic vassal, as it was before the Pig War.

choices.text: Put off any bargain with Vienna, and rebuild the exhausted army with French loans and Russian rifles and ammunition
choices.why: Lean on Vienna’s market again and Serbia invites another Pig War
choices.after: The Paris banks agreed to a new loan, and St Petersburg promised rifles and ammunition. Vienna concluded that Serbia was preparing for the next war.

choices.text: As Pacu urges, sign a new trade and railway agreement with Vienna to rescue the treasury, and reopen trade on the Bosnian border
choices.why: Railways and schools in the new territories will be paid for by the market next door
choices.after: The trade agreement passed parliament by a narrow margin. Livestock began moving through the border markets again, but former journalists of Pijemont sneered that the dream of South Slav unification had been sold for the price of pigs.

note.text: Pašić’s circular telegram of 19 July 1914 stated that, to improve relations with Austria-Hungary, the Serbian government had been settling the question of the Oriental Railway, new rail links, and the transit across Serbia of Austro-Hungarian goods bound for Constantinople, Sofia, Salonika and Athens.

RS-08G.title: Unconditional Acceptance
RS-08G.clock: 15 minutes to the deadline for a reply
RS-08G.scene: The reply you hand over contains no conditions and no reservations. Minister Giesl, whose bags were all packed, reads it twice. In Vienna the chief of the General Staff, Conrad, rages that Serbia must be attacked all the same, and Berlin frets that Vienna will let the opportunity slip. In the officers’ club in Belgrade the word “betrayal” goes around, and the regent says nothing all day.

voices.text: The day Austrian officials interrogate Serbian officers, the officers will not sit idle. Nor can anyone promise, Prime Minister, that you will live through that day unharmed.
Prime Minister, a promise made must be kept. Give Vienna another pretext, and this time it will not be a note that comes but guns.

choices.text: Keep the promise, as the regent says: arrest Tankosić that night and prepare to receive Austrian investigators at the border
choices.why: Break the promise, and next time it will be guns that come, not a note
choices.after: Tankosić was arrested that night, and preparations began at the border to receive the Austrian investigators.

choices.text: Accept in writing, but slow the implementation by sending parliament the legal changes needed to admit the investigators
choices.why: Legal procedure can put off the day of humiliation
choices.after: The Serbian Ministry of Justice replied that it would send parliament the legal changes needed to admit the investigators. Vienna’s hard-liners welcomed it, saying Serbia had shown its true face.

note.text: Giesl had instructions to break off relations and leave at once unless Serbia accepted unconditionally. In fact he spent only a few minutes skimming the reply.

RS-09G.title: The Austrian Investigators
RS-09G.scene: The Austrian investigators have arrived in Belgrade. The statements of the Sarajevo defendants in their hands lead from the railway official Ciganović to Major Tankosić and on to those above him. Everyone knows that at the end of the inquiry stands Apis, the chief of intelligence on the General Staff. The Russian chargé d’affaires makes no secret of his discomfort, saying the Serbian government is abasing itself too far.

voices.text: Hand over Apis and the army collapses. End it with a few of the officers below him.
We must go all the way. If the society is not finished this time, Serbia will remain forever a country with two governments.

choices.text: As Stefanović says, hand over only a few junior officers, and shield Apis and the society’s leaders on grounds of military secrecy
choices.why: Handing over Apis would bring down the army, so the top must be protected
choices.after: The investigators reported to Vienna that the inquiry had stopped short of the top. Conrad declared that he now held proof that Serbia had broken its promise.

choices.text: As Protić says, put even Apis before a Serbian court, and allow the Austrian investigators to attend the proceedings
choices.why: Fail to finish the society now, and the country remains with two governments
choices.after: On the day Apis was arrested, shots rang out in several Belgrade barracks, but the Royal Guard stood by the regent.

note.text: In its actual reply the Serbian government stated that it had arrested Tankosić, but said of Ciganović that “it has not yet been possible to arrest him,” adding that a warrant had been issued. It has been claimed that he slipped out of Belgrade with the tacit consent of the authorities.

RS-10G.title: An Election After Surrender
RS-10G.scene: On election day the Independent Radicals and the nationalist papers call you “Vienna’s prime minister,” and the officers talk openly of a coup. Yet many peasants who lost sons and brothers in the two Balkan Wars are relieved to have escaped a third war. When the white-bearded old prime minister mounts the platform, his voice hoarse, he is met with jeers and applause together.

voices.text: Postpone the election and declare martial law. The dynasty and the government must be protected before the officers move.
Postpone the election and people will say a government that surrendered has lost its nerve as well. Put the price of peace to the people directly and accept their judgment.

choices.text: On Protić’s advice, hold the election as scheduled and leave the people to judge a peace bought with humiliation
choices.why: Only if the people set the price of peace themselves can the government justify holding on
choices.after: The Radicals lost many seats but kept power. Serbia had chosen to endure a long season of humiliation instead of war.

choices.text: As the regent demands, declare martial law, postpone the election, and put down the officers plotting a coup first
choices.why: The dynasty and the government must be protected before the officers move
choices.after: Troops filled the streets of Belgrade. The parliamentary government established after 1903 came to a halt for the first time.

note.text: Between the 1903 coup and 1914, parliamentary government took root in Serbia, and the period is sometimes called the “golden age” of Serbian democracy, but the problem of the army’s interference in politics never went away.

RS-08R.title: Rejection
RS-08R.scene: You hand Giesl a short reply rejecting the note in its entirety. Giesl leaves as planned on the 6:30 p.m. train, but this time the tone of the European press is different. The British foreign secretary, Grey, had hoped Serbia would accept what it could, and the Russian foreign minister, Sazonov, had also urged Serbia to be as cautious as possible. Vienna proclaims that Serbia chose war of its own accord.

voices.text: Sazonov is deeply displeased. He says Serbia has handed Vienna its pretext in front of Europe. Even so, Russian public opinion is still on Serbia’s side.
There is no retreat now. Order mobilization in the king’s name, and we go to Niš.

choices.text: Offer Sazonov no explanation, and declare in the king’s name that Serbia will fight to the end, alone if need be
choices.why: A small country can rely not on explanations but on its resolve to fight
choices.after: Every train to Niš rang with soldiers’ songs. In St Petersburg there were complaints that Serbia was trying to drag Russia into war.

choices.text: Mobilize and go to Niš, and seek Russia’s understanding through a personal letter from the regent explaining the rejection
choices.why: If Serbia cannot win back a displeased Russia, it will be left alone
choices.after: The regent’s second letter pleaded that not only Point 6 but the entire note had been incompatible with the dignity of an independent state. Nicholas II delayed his answer.

note.text: In fact, on 24 July Grey told the Austrian ambassador that the note “seemed to me the most formidable document I had ever seen addressed by one State to another that was independent.” Serbia’s actual reply, which accepted most of the demands, helped keep that sympathy.

RS-09R.title: The Capital Under Fire
RS-09R.scene: War was declared on 28 July, and since the early hours of the 29th Belgrade has been under bombardment. Russia has announced partial mobilization of four military districts near the Austrian border, but in St Petersburg there is talk that Serbia threw away the chance of reconciliation. In London, Grey keeps proposing mediation by four powers.

voices.text: It is not too late. Accept Grey’s proposal for mediation, and announce that you will reconsider the points you rejected.
Talking of negotiation on the day shells fall on the capital is surrender. Hold out until Russia moves.

choices.text: As Crackanthorpe urges, accept Grey’s mediation and announce a new reply revising the points Serbia rejected
choices.why: To stop the shelling, better to admit that the first reply was a mistake
choices.after: Vienna replied that it would negotiate only after occupying Belgrade. Russia halted at partial mobilization and watched the conference in London.

choices.text: As the regent wishes, reject mediation even under bombardment, and hold out at Niš until Russia enters the war
choices.why: Talk of negotiation under the shells would only be read as surrender
choices.after: Serbia held out, and everything now rested on the decision in St Petersburg.

note.text: Russia decided on 28 July on partial mobilization of the four military districts of Odessa, Kiev, Moscow and Kazan, and announced it on the 29th. The Russian military had wanted general mobilization from the start, arguing that partial mobilization was technically difficult.

RS-08T.title: An Attempt to Buy Time
RS-08T.clock: Half a day to the deadline for a reply
RS-08T.event: The same day in Vienna, the Russian chargé d’affaires asked for an extension of the deadline, but the Austrian government refused.
RS-08T.scene: You send someone to the Austrian legation to ask that the deadline be put back a few days, and to ask exactly what Points 5 and 6 mean. Minister Giesl’s answer is brief: he has no authority to discuss the contents of the note, nor to change the deadline. As it becomes clear that Vienna drafted the document not as a starting point for negotiation but as a demand for unconditional acceptance, the 6 p.m. deadline draws near.

voices.who: Laza Pacu (Finance Minister and Acting Prime Minister)
voices.text: Vienna never meant to negotiate. All that is left is how we word the reply.
If we cannot gain time, we must at least keep the moral case on Serbia’s side. Europe will read this reply.

choices.text: When Giesl refuses to negotiate, rewrite the reply just before the deadline to accept everything, Point 6 included, and avoid war
choices.why: With the road to negotiation closed, humiliation is better than bombardment
choices.after: After 5 p.m. you rewrote the reply. As the sentence accepting Point 6 went in, several ministers walked out of the room.

choices.text: As the regent says, keep the moral case on Serbia’s side: go back to a reply that accepts most demands and rejects Point 6
choices.why: If time cannot be bought, build the moral case in a reply that Europe will read
choices.after: When the request for an extension was refused, you went back to the course of the reply Serbia actually sent. The attempt to buy time failed, but the diplomatic papers of Europe now record that Vienna refused to negotiate.

note.text: In fact, on 24 July the Russian foreign minister, Sazonov, instructed Kudashev, the chargé d’affaires in Vienna, to request an extension of the deadline, and Vienna refused on 25 July. Minister Giesl already had instructions to break off relations and leave unless the acceptance was unconditional.

epilogues.A: In the general election of August 1914 the Radicals held on to power despite charges that they had “bowed to Vienna,” and with the collapse of Apis’s society Serbia became, for the first time, a country whose army obeyed its government. But the question of the South Slavs of Bosnia and the hostility with Austria remained. In fact, in 1917 Pašić, then in exile on Corfu, promised a unified South Slav state together with Croat and Slovene representatives; had peace lasted, that unification might have become a matter not of war but of long negotiation.
epilogues.B: The Austrian army halted, holding Belgrade as a pledge, and Serbia kept its independence but had to await the verdict of a conference of the great powers with its capital surrendered. The officer corps and the nationalists branded Pašić’s government the author of the humiliation, and men like Apis may even have gained strength. As in the Bosnian annexation crisis of 1908–1909, Serbia’s resentment was simply put off until the next crisis.
epilogues.E: The Serbian army drove out the Austro-Hungarian forces at Mount Cer in August 1914 and again at the Battle of the Kolubara in December, recapturing Belgrade, but in 1915, after typhus had swept the country, it was attacked in October by Germany, Austria-Hungary and Bulgaria together. Regent Alexander and Pašić, the old King Peter riding in an oxcart, and Field Marshal Putnik carried in a sedan chair led the army and the refugees in midwinter across the mountains of Montenegro and Albania to the Adriatic, and the survivors were taken by Allied ships to the island of Corfu and then returned to the Salonika front. On 26 June 1917 Apis was shot after being sentenced by a court-martial at Salonika (he was rehabilitated at a retrial in 1953); in July of the same year Pašić promised a unified South Slav state in the Corfu Declaration; and on 1 December 1918 in Belgrade Regent Alexander proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. The dead numbered some 730,000 to 750,000 according to demographic studies (Serbia and Montenegro combined), or about 1.25 million according to the Serbian estimate submitted to the Paris Peace Conference in 1919; the figures vary widely, from about one-sixth to more than one-quarter of a prewar population of about 4.5 million. On any reckoning, Serbia is counted as the belligerent that suffered the heaviest losses in proportion to its population.
epilogues.F: The peace of 1914 did not last more than a few years. Serbia rearmed, Russia completed the arms buildup of its “Great Programme,” aimed at 1917, and in the next Balkan crisis Europe faced off again with even larger armies. Even Pašić’s government, having put down Apis, might never have managed to control a new generation of officers and students crying out for unification.
epilogues.G: Serbia avoided war, but as the price of accepting Austrian officials into investigations on its own soil it had to give up the dignity of an independent state and part of its sovereignty. Amid the officers’ backlash and the threat of a coup, the Radical government held on precariously, and Pan-Slavists mocked a Serbia that had lost Russia’s trust as “Vienna’s satellite.” Even so, Serbia was spared what the war that was actually fought cost it: the deaths of one-sixth to one-quarter of its prewar population.

dossier.t: Born in 1845 in Zaječar in eastern Serbia, you studied engineering at the Polytechnic in Zurich, where you were drawn to radical politics. Sentenced to death in absentia after the Timok rebellion of 1883, you lived in exile in Bulgaria; under the Obrenović dynasty you were imprisoned and made a statement admitting that the Radical Party had been disloyal to the royal house. For this, younger party members called you a coward, and the party even split. After the 1903 coup, as parliamentary politics took hold, you led the Radical Party and headed several governments. Taciturn and never in a hurry to decide, you have been criticized for letting hard problems drag on until events solve them, yet praised as a party organizer without equal.

The twenty-five-year-old regent, Alexander, sided with you and the Radicals throughout the crisis of spring 1914 and deeply distrusts Apis’s faction. Interior Minister Stojan Protić, a champion of civilian supremacy, pushed through the Priority Decree, and Finance Minister Laza Pacu is an old comrade who runs the government when you are away. Hartwig, the Russian minister in Belgrade since 1909, is the patron who helped you design the Balkan League; he was said to stray from his instructions and present his own views as Russia’s official position, but he dies suddenly on 10 July. A contemporary later wrote that you relied on Hartwig in diplomacy and on Pacu in domestic affairs. And standing against the government is Apis, chief of intelligence on the General Staff, a leading figure of the 1903 coup and leader of the Black Hand.

Your greatest fear is the exhausted army. By one estimate more than 36,000 soldiers were killed and some 55,000 seriously wounded in the two Balkan Wars, and rifles and shells fall far short of what a mobilized army needs. Governing newly won Macedonia and Kosovo has brought you into conflict with the officer corps, and you must also keep the army from destabilizing the government before the August election. Across the border in Bosnia, most of the tenant farmers (kmets) who pay rent to Muslim landlords are Serb peasants, and since the annexation of 1908 resentment of Austrian rule has spread among young students. Your hope is to consolidate the new territories through a few years of peace, build up the country with French capital and Russian patronage, and one day unite in a single state with the Serbs, and beyond them the South Slavs, of Austria-Hungary.

movers.intro: Historians differ on how Serbian anti-Austrian feeling took shape, whether Pašić’s government could have controlled it, and whether Serbia was no more than Russia’s proxy. The main views are these.
views: Christopher Clark: argues that after the 1903 coup Serbian politics were deeply entangled with the aspiration to national unification and with secret societies of officers. He stresses that Pašić’s government knew about the young men who crossed the border but lacked the power and the will to cut the society’s network, and that this was the starting point of the July Crisis.

Vladimir Dedijer: in The Road to Sarajevo (1966) he explained the assassination above all as the product of the grievances of Bosnian peasant society and the revolutionary mood of the younger generation. He emphasizes that the officers in Belgrade supplied weapons and a route rather than creating the young men’s resolve.

Dušan T. Bataković: sees Serbia in 1903–1914 as a “fragile but functional democracy” that worked despite unconstitutional pressure from the army, and stresses that the contest between Pašić and the Black Hand went on right up to the eve of Sarajevo. He also points out that on 24 June Pašić ordered an investigation of the border guards and of Apis.

Zoran Bajin: argues that Spalajković in St Petersburg reported the Russian mood with fervor and at times excessive optimism, and that his reports made the Serbian leadership more determined to resist Vienna’s demands. He also brought to light that the Russian chargé d’affaires, Strandtmann, used his discretion not to pass on to the Serbian government the Council of Ministers’ advice not to resist if Serbia could not hold off an invasion.
movers.note: During the war Austria and Germany portrayed Serbia as Russia’s puppet, but the facts that Hartwig often strayed from his instructions and that Russia did not back Serbia to the end in the Albanian crisis of 1913 show that the relationship was not one-sided. Some scholars point out that whether the government could have calmed anti-Austrian feeling must be judged against the constraints of a constitution guaranteeing freedom of the press, the power of the officer corps, and the August election.
